english: At times we must interpret a word according to its plain meaning, at others figuratively, and occasionally because the context requires a different sense—either as it stands or as it appears elsewhere in Scripture. By observing this carefully, we avoid many mistakes and unfounded suppositions. Therefore, we must recognize that what has been perceived is not always located in the same reality; sometimes it is bodily sight, sometimes spiritual discernment. This principle must be universally understood: when the divine purpose is to conceal truth rather than reveal it openly to the Spirit in the prophets and to the Word of Christ in the apostles, the phrasing often becomes complex and does not follow a single, straightforward sequence. This is done so that the unworthy, upon encountering what is secretly reserved for their benefit, do not bring judgment upon themselves by seizing what was meant to remain hidden. This is frequently the reason why some suppose that Scripture as a whole lacks syntax and coherence—especially the prophetic and apostolic writings, and most notably Paul’s letter to the Romans, where legal matters are named differently and placed in varied contexts, making it seem as though Paul deviates from his stated purpose. But what shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness had the law not declared, 'You shall not covet.' Thus we understand the law not merely as Moses’ prohibition against covetousness, but also as the natural law ingrained in us—for desire is naturally implanted in us as a passion, and sin has seized opportunity not only through the written commandment but also through this inner law. Even Adam knew this before the Mosaic law. Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness—not only in me, but in every soul when sin awakens, all covetousness wages war against the human race; for it is impossible for a human soul not to fall into passions, even if later, through discipline, it appears, as it were, to attain impassibility. Paul declares that all covetousness is passionate and sinful—which the law forbids by teaching, 'You shall not covet'—and this is an irrational impulse arising from mere urge, overflowing beyond reason, by which we cling to life, desiring good, the middling and indifferent life, attaching ourselves to wealth, honor, women, and other covetous things, doing the will of sin, thus stretching ourselves toward what we imagine to be good upon all that we desire. For the fantasy of good becomes covetousness. Apart from the law, sin is powerless. I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died, and I found that the very commandment meant for life became death to me—for sin, seizing opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and thereby killed me. Then it could be said of such a person that he lives apart from the law; for upon this condition, reflecting, Paul and every person would say, I once lived apart from the law, when, as he says, on the eighth day after birth, of the race of Israel, a Hebrew of the Hebrews—for it is not possible for an irrational infant, possessing a state, to live under law. Indeed, every person has lived apart from the law at some time, namely in childhood, when there was no reproof, for ignorance is not subject to punishment; and the commandment has come at some time to every person—but when did they fulfill the word, and understand the commandment enjoining such things and forbidding such things? And at the very moment the commandment came, in its first occurrence, wickedness arose—or, as Paul called it, sin awoke, having been dead; for since it is not natural for sin and humanity to coexist, therefore, when the commandment came, sin awoke and the soul died, according to the soul, the sinner, this one shall die. english: The goodness embedded in the law, meant to guide life, paradoxically becomes a catalyst for death—since sin lacks definition apart from the law, and condemnation requires its boundary, yet it is through the law that sin’s guilt and punishment are formally established. Do not confuse the initial death of sin with its final demise; there is a profound distinction between sin lying inert without the law’s demand and sin being put to death through the Spirit’s mortification of our earthly nature; thus, the lifeless state of sin in each scenario produces vastly different outcomes in spiritual vitality, and they cannot be equated by any measure of lived experience. Indeed, sin remains deadly as long as our bodily impulses remain un subdued by the divine word, and even before the law was given, sin held sway over humanity. Yet someone might object: even if sin seizes the commandment as an occasion to deceive and destroy, we must still affirm the truth and embrace the law inscribed on the heart by God as holy, and honor the command as good, flowing from the God of goodness. So, has this good become death to me? Certainly not! But sin, in order to be exposed as sin through the very good that works death in me, so that through the commandment sin might be revealed as utterly sinful. If someone objects, saying, 'Perhaps the holy law has become death to humanity?'—know this: when the commandment arrived, sin sprang back to life and the person died—let them understand that it was not the good that turned into death, but that sin must be made manifest in its true evilness; for when the good dwells in the soul, evil is unveiled, and if one then sins, it becomes clear that the commandment, which identified evil and warned against it, serves as the occasion of death, and sin—not merely sin, but sin in its most aggravated form—enters through the holy command and brings about our destruction. We acknowledge that the law is spiritual, yet I remain fleshly, enslaved to sin. A question emerges from all this: how can Paul say these things without appearing to contradict himself when he declares we were bought with a price, Christ redeemed us, and yet I no longer live, but Christ lives in me? Unless we allow that the Word assumes different persons, and the passages are tailored to distinct personal realities, in which the foolish act contrary to their original intent. This discourse is fitting for those who have come to know the law as divine and see its commands as good, yet, as those still enslaved to sin and governed by the flesh, they do not know how to resist and thus fall into transgression. For what I do, I do not understand; for what I wish to do, I do not do, but what I detest, that I perform. These words suit those who have weakened toward passion due to feeble reasoning, and those who, at times, are overcome by anger and fear and act against their will and their deepest aversions; but when, having been defeated by intellectual pride, we are conquered by what appears good but is not true, we endorse the law in word while doing what pleases us. For I delight in God’s law according to the inner self, yet I perceive another law in my members waging war against the law of my mind and leading me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my flesh. In those who have not yet fortified themselves toward virtue, Paul outlines this present reality: just as a soldier who has taken captive enemies leads them away, so in these individuals, the law in their members opposes the law of their mind, enslaves the miserable soul, and drives it toward the law of sin residing in the bodily members. Miserable man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. As one who weakens the human frailty that drags and distracts reason and incites opposition, he cries, 'Wretched man that I am'; and as one delivered by divine aid from the body named the body of death for these very reasons, he adds, 'I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ.' For what the law could not accomplish—because it was weakened by the flesh—

english: [[God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, and condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit >> Bible:Romans 8:3-4]].

Here he speaks of what the law of sin and death cannot do. Virtue is strong by its own nature; vice and what comes from it are weak and powerless. Vice rules not the strong but the slack—not by its own strength but by their feebleness. Such a 'law' is powerless by nature, so it worked in weak flesh.

God condemned that law by sending his Son not in flesh of the sin that slaves of the law of sin serve, but in a likeness of such flesh. The Son's flesh was not sin but likeness, because it did not come from a man's seed and a woman joined in sleep. So God condemned sin become exceedingly sinful, and through the flesh the divine law's righteous requirement is fulfilled in us when we do not walk according to flesh—where that powerless weakness, which is vice, works—but follow God according to his Spirit and receive the Son into ourselves.

[[Because the mindset of the flesh is enmity toward God, for it is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God >> Bible:Romans 8:7-8]]. From Paul we learn who walk according to flesh—those who mind fleshly things—and who according to Spirit—those who mind the Spirit's things.

Fleshly mindsets are fornication, wantonness, idolatry, and the like—death itself. The Spirit's fruit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, and what follows—life. Such people are already in life and rejoice in peace. Those who sow to the flesh reap corruption; those who live by the Spirit sow of the Spirit and reap eternal life. Those of the flesh's mindset are also God's enemies.

People who want riches or glory also mind fleshly things. Jews who live by the letter and practice visible circumcision in the flesh mind the fleshly side of the law; Jews in secret, who circumcise heart and spirit, mind the Spirit's things. In the fleshly mindset of the law you find death and enmity toward God; in the Spirit's mindset of the law, life and peace. Those in the flesh of the law cannot please God; those in the Spirit of the law can. Both profess Moses' law, yet they take it according to flesh and we according to Spirit—so they reckon the promises fleshy, while we take them as spiritual blessing in the heavenlies.

[[Hope that is seen is not hope; for what one sees, why still hope? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with endurance >> Bible:Romans 8:24-25]]. Other copies read something like 'if he is eager he endures what he sees'; but greatness belongs to the one who hopes toward what is unseen and, stretching the mind toward it, endures whatever comes.

[[Likewise the Spirit helps our weaknesses; for we do not know what we ought to pray, but the Spirit itself intercedes for us with unspoken groanings >> Bible:Romans 8:26]]. It fills up what our weakness lacks. Through this, all human nature is shown. In countless ways the Spirit helps our weakness, not least when we pray and cross over so as to pray in spirit. Not knowing what to pray as we ought, helped by the Spirit we pray in spirit; then with the mind following that help we pray with the mind too. Prayer that uses only one is incomplete, as [[if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful >> Bible:1 Corinthians 14:14]] shows. So that the mind may bear fruit, he says: I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind. [[What then… >> Bible:Romans 8:31]]…

english: What can we say in response? If God stands with us, who can stand against us? He who did not withhold his own Son but delivered him for our sake—how could he fail to lavish upon us, together with him, every good thing? This is a recapitulation, a return to what has gone before, and he speaks not in defiance of what is plainly evident. I have seen, moreover, how all things rise against us for the sake of that name—people, yes, but also the very forces that oppose: principalities, powers, world-rulers of this dark age, and the spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly realms, with Satan himself bent on our overthrow. Yet we must not claim, contrary to what is evident, that if God is for us, then his cause is insignificant and we are nothing, or that our adversaries are powerless; to think so would be to invite fear and distress, as if we were left alone to contend with such foes. But now that God is for us, what measure can be taken against this array of opposition? To what shall they be compared—if not to nothing? Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen? God himself, who justifies. Who is there to condemn? It seems clear that this points to the devil, the accuser of the brethren, who charges the elect before God—yet there is not one he accuses who is not also defended, save only Jesus, who knew no sin. And so it is said: the ruler of this world comes, and finds in me nothing to lay hold of. Thus he is brought to nothing by his own accusations against God’s elect, for if God justifies, who can condemn? Even if the accuser produces the very things for which they were once condemned—if they had not been left behind—still, God has justified them: as a cloud sweeps away their iniquities, as darkness is scattered before light, as those once stained by sin are made white like refined zinc. Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For the victor in a contest is not merely the one who, after struggle, overtakes his opponent, but the one who does not even allow the beginning of resistance to take shape. Such was Paul, and such are those who have undergone the same preparation against temptation: they trample oppression, find joy in the one who straitens, pursue the hunter by endurance, laugh at famine through heavenly food, regard nakedness as nothing, having put on Christ through whom they are clothed, treat danger as no danger, and wield the sword not by strength but by the living word of God, which they find easy to wield, being persuaded. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Consider whether it is not reasonable that I am convinced of this—having appointed these things to be weighed against greater realities, or measured by human trials—and that the very thing that would separate us is nothing but the esteeming of the lesser exercises of the human soul over the greater. And if we more than conquer the former and the human, we shall not lack a better breath and energy surrounding them; thus it was fitting that Paul added the words 'through him who loved us.' But reflect: if death indeed sought to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, it would not be the common fate of which it was said above—that we die wholly each day—but rather the enemy of Christ, who has been destroyed. For this one would seek to divide us, to speak, Paul—but he shall not be destroyed by the one in whom he dwells, Christ. And life is not contrary to this death, for mutually opposed things do not naturally desire the same end; rather, the way of life through sin, its appearances, and falsehood is what opposes it. But if even for each kind of sin there is some base form of life, you will know this through the superior mercy that extends over life. For this one would seek to separate the one embraced in the love of God in Christ Jesus—but she cannot, being destroyed in part by the death through which one dies on account of sin, and in part by our life, which is hidden in Christ in God. And the angels, too, seek to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, concerning whom it has been said to those on the left: 'Depart, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.' And the thing that neither rulers nor what is in us—the old blood and barrier—can effect, but which, before the rulers and the things that follow, is referred back.

english: Next comes the clause [[when he abolishes every rule and every authority and power >> Bible:1 Corinthians 15:24]]. After that stand 'the things present.' Ask whether these can point to the world-ruler of this darkness, and not merely to present human affairs; another reader would refer 'present things' to what is seen and temporary.

Then consider what 'the things to come' are. They may be the struggles still ahead for the apostle in this life's sojourn, measured from the days when the letter was written; or they may be what meets the soul at once after this age and after departure—when the ruler of this world and powers under him will try to seize the one who has gone abroad, yet cannot touch those who have already laid hold of the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Next after these is 'neither powers,' which seems to name a kind of rational being outside a mortal body.

english: —and the appetite for contemplation seems to be hunger and thirst, as things that work health in the soul. If the enemy ever feels that hunger or thirst after repenting of his sins, the holy person must give him the holy bread when he hungers—unless he is a dog or pig unworthy of holy things.

There are many ways to feed a hungry enemy: sometimes by a teaching word, sometimes by prayer for him. And since [[the head of every man is Christ >> Bible:1 Corinthians 11:3]], the enemy—as not a 'man' because of impiety—has the antichrist as head. That head must be consumed as opposed to the Word of God by the coals of rational fire, whenever the impious one whose head is the antichrist, hungering, eats—

english: —the bread from what is holy, and when thirsty is given living water from the holy spring. So it is a fine work to heap coals—that is, chosen words—on the enemy's head. The Lord Jesus consumes that head [[with the spirit of his mouth >> Bible:2 Thessalonians 2:8]]; this is the saving fire of which he said, [[I came to cast fire on the earth >> Bible:Luke 12:49]]—meaning the consuming and vanishing of all that is bodily and material.

Many coals are needed so the enemy's head may be thoroughly burned away; they are the true words that make falsehood vanish. When that head is consumed or mastered by the heaped coals, feeding the hungry enemy turns the former enemy into a friend who now has Christ as head.
